blocks.text: The examiner may ask:
**“Examine this child generally and report your findings.”**
Or:
**“Perform a general examination of this child.”**
Your job is to demonstrate that you can **assess the child's overall condition before moving to a system-specific examination.**

subsections.subsection_title: 1. What you should be able to do

blocks.title: By the end of this station, you should be able to assess:

blocks.text: And importantly:
**Recognize a sick child early.**
“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I am going to examine your child. Is that okay?”
For infants, allow the child to remain with the caregiver where possible.
Perform hand hygiene.
**Observe before touching.**
The child may reveal a lot before you perform a single examination maneuver.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. First impression — from the end of the bed

blocks.text: Stand back and observe.
Ask yourself:

content_groups.group_title: Is the child well or ill?

blocks.text: You should be able to say:
“This child appears comfortable and is alert and appropriately interactive.”
Or:
“This child appears ill, lethargic and in moderate respiratory distress.”
Look at the child's:
In infants, listen to the cry.
A **high-pitched cry** may be associated with neurological pathology.
A weak cry may indicate severe illness, weakness or neurological impairment.
For an OSCE, don't simply say:
“The child is conscious.”
Describe the level more precisely.
A quick pediatric assessment:
**A — Alert**
**V — Responds to Voice**
**P — Responds to Pain**
**U — Unresponsive**
For a sick child, AVPU is a useful rapid assessment.
Look for:
Look for loss of subcutaneous fat.
Do not diagnose malnutrition purely by looking.
This is extremely important in pediatrics.
Look at:
Ask:
“Has the child been producing tears when crying?”
Gently pinch appropriate skin.
Assess how quickly it returns.
Press on the nail bed or sternum and assess the return of colour.
Normally approximately **≤2 seconds** in a warm child.
Ask the caregiver:
“How much has the child been passing urine?”
Reduced urine output is concerning.
**Dehydration ≠ shock.**
A child can be dehydrated without being in shock.
Shock is a **circulatory failure** and requires urgent assessment and treatment.
Inspect:
Gently pull down the lower eyelid.
Inspect:
Ask the child to look up or gently examine the sclera.
Look for yellow discoloration.
In a newborn, **jaundice requires a much more structured assessment**, which we'll cover in the newborn examination.
Central cyanosis suggests significant arterial desaturation.
Peripheral cyanosis can occur with poor peripheral perfusion or cold exposure.
**Do not diagnose central cyanosis simply by looking at the nail beds.**
The tongue/oral mucosa is more useful for central cyanosis.
Look at the fingers.
Ask the child to place corresponding fingers together.
Normally there is a diamond-shaped window.
Loss of the window suggests clubbing.
Then test for **pitting oedema**.
Hold for several seconds.
Release and observe whether a pit remains.
**Bilateral pitting oedema in a malnourished child is particularly important.**
Palpate relevant lymph node groups.
For an enlarged node, describe:
**S C M T M**
**Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy is particularly concerning** and should not be dismissed.
Look systematically.
**Non-blanching petechiae/purpura + fever = consider meningococcal/severe bacterial infection until proven otherwise.**
Look at the child's:
You don't need to diagnose a syndrome simply from one feature.
Say:
“The child has dysmorphic features, including…”
Then describe them.
This is **one of the most important parts of general pediatric examination**.
Look at the child before touching them.
Count for a full minute, particularly in infants and young children.
**An exhausted child with decreasing respiratory effort may actually be getting worse, not** **better.**

subsections.subsection_title: 18. Assess circulation and look for shock

blocks.text: Look at:
Normally approximately ≤2 seconds under appropriate conditions.
Ask about urine output.
Altered consciousness may indicate poor cerebral perfusion.

items.text: Hypotension — **usually a late sign in children**

blocks.text: **A normal blood pressure does not exclude shock in a child.**
Children can maintain blood pressure through compensatory mechanisms until relatively late.
Measure temperature using an appropriate method.
**Hypothermia in a sick infant or young child can be a sign of serious infection**, not simply “being cold.”
Pain assessment should be **age appropriate**.
Ask:
“Where does it hurt?”
Use an appropriate pain scale.
Useful particularly for young/non-verbal children:
**F — Face**
**L — Legs**
**A — Activity**
**C — Cry**
**C — Consolability**
You should know that **normal values vary significantly with age**.
**The younger the child, the higher the normal heart and respiratory rates tend to be.**
And:
**Normal pediatric blood pressure is age/size dependent.**
Don't rely on a single adult-style BP threshold.
We will cover the **age-specific normal pediatric vital signs and BP interpretation** separately because they are important enough to warrant their own OSCE section.

subsections.subsection_title: 22. What else should you look for?

blocks.text: Depending on the child and station:
In an OSCE, you can think:
**LOOK → TALK → COLOUR → HYDRATION → NUTRITION → NODES → SKIN → BREATHING → CIRCULATION → VITALS**
Or more practically:

content_groups.group_title: At the end of the bed

blocks.text:
**1.** General appearance
**2.** Consciousness
**3.** Behaviour/interaction
**4.** Respiratory effort
**5.** Colour
**6.** Nutritional state
**7.** Hydration

**8.** Hands
**9.** Pulse/capillary refill
**10.** Pallor
**11.** Cyanosis
**12.** Clubbing
**13.** Oedema
**14.** Lymph nodes
**15.** Skin
**16.** Eyes/mouth
**17.** Dysmorphic features

**18.** Temperature
**19.** Respiratory rate
**20.** Oxygen saturation
**21.** Blood pressure
**22.** Weight/height/MUAC when appropriate
Then proceed to the **relevant systemic examination**.
This is where you can gain easy marks.
Don't say:
“The child is fine.”
Instead:

“This is a 5-year-old boy who is alert, comfortable and appropriately interactive with his caregiver. He is not in obvious respiratory distress. He is pink, warm and well perfused, with no peripheral or central cyanosis, pallor, jaundice or clubbing. There is no clinically significant peripheral oedema or generalized lymphadenopathy. His nutritional status appears appropriate for age.”
Then add your vital signs:

“His respiratory rate is 24 breaths per minute, pulse rate is 100 beats per minute, oxygen saturation is 98% on room air, temperature is 36.8°C and blood pressure is appropriate for his age and size.”
Then:
“I would proceed to a focused systemic examination based on the presenting complaint.”
Suppose you have a child with severe pneumonia:

“This is a 2-year-old child who appears acutely ill and lethargic, with marked respiratory distress characterized by tachypnoea, nasal flaring and subcostal and intercostal recession. The child is centrally pink with no obvious cyanosis. There is reduced peripheral perfusion with prolonged capillary refill and cool extremities. The child appears mildly dehydrated. I would urgently assess the airway, breathing and circulation and proceed with a focused respiratory and cardiovascular examination.”
That sounds much more clinically mature than simply listing findings.

content_groups.group_title: Q1. What are signs of severe respiratory distress?

blocks.text: **Answer:**
Tachypnoea, marked chest recession, nasal flaring, grunting, use of accessory muscles, cyanosis, inability to feed or speak appropriately, altered consciousness and exhaustion.

content_groups.group_title: Q2. What are signs of shock in a child?

blocks.text: Tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, cool extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, oliguria and hypotension, although hypotension is generally a late sign.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What is the difference between central and peripheral cyanosis?

blocks.text: **Central cyanosis** involves the tongue and oral mucosa and indicates significant arterial desaturation. **Peripheral cyanosis** is mainly seen in the extremities and can occur with peripheral vasoconstriction or poor circulation.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. How do you assess dehydration?

blocks.text: By assessing mental status, thirst/drinking ability, eyes, mucous membranes, tears, skin turgor, capillary refill and urine output, while considering the overall clinical picture.

content_groups.group_title: Q5. What are causes of generalized lymphadenopathy in a child?
Q6. What are causes of clubbing in children?
Q7. What are causes of oedema in a child?

blocks.text: Think:
**Renal + nutritional + cardiac + hepatic**

content_groups.group_title: ❌ 1. Starting with examination without observing the child

blocks.text: You lose an opportunity to identify respiratory distress, shock, dehydration and altered consciousness.
Respiratory rate is **one of the most important pediatric vital signs**.
In young children, respiratory rate can be irregular.
**Count for a full minute.**

content_groups.group_title: ❌ 4. Calling a child “well” without assessing interaction

blocks.text: A child who is unusually quiet or lethargic may be seriously ill.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ 5. Checking only the nail beds for cyanosis

blocks.text: Always assess the **oral mucosa/tongue for central cyanosis**.
Look for wasting and oedema, then objectively assess growth.

content_groups.group_title: ❌ 7. Assuming normal BP means no shock

blocks.text: **Hypotension can be late in pediatric shock.**
Expose only what is necessary and preserve dignity.
Use the **least distressing examination first**.
For example, examine the chest before forcing an upset child to open their mouth.
A very useful rule:
**“Observe first, examine gently, leave the uncomfortable parts until later.”**

blocks.title: Children often become distressed when you:

blocks.text: So use the child's cooperation wisely.
For example, if you need to examine a crying toddler:
**Listen to the chest while the child is relatively calm → examine the heart → abdomen → neurological/general observations → leave throat/ears until later.**

content_groups.group_title: What you should memorize from this station

blocks.text: If the examiner says:
**“Examine this child generally.”**
Your mental checklist should immediately be:

**Appearance → Consciousness → Interaction → Nutrition → Hydration → Pallor → Jaundice → Cyanosis → Clubbing → Oedema → Lymph nodes → Skin → Dysmorphism → Respiratory distress → Perfusion/shock → Vital signs.**
